stem: 28-year-old female presented with severe epigastric pain and epigastric tenderness, labs revealed amylase 1253 UI and normal LFTs + multiple gallstones in US and mild intrahepatic biliary dilatation. After 3 days the patient improved clinically and amylase returned to the normal level. What is the next appropriate management?
srcNote: (Pancreas) Source note (Final 433 A Q6 (p. 177)): Cholecystectomy at the same admission to not have another attack of pancreatitis.
expl: Mild gallstone pancreatitis (normal LFTs, stone passed) → cholecystectomy during the same admission once settled — waiting 6–8 weeks risks recurrence (~30%).

why.D: ERCP only for retained CBD stone/cholangitis.

stem: A 56-year-old female with suspected choledocholithiasis undergoes ERCP, which reveals biliary stones without bile duct wall thickening. Six hours after the procedure, she develops severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, associated with nausea and vomiting. Laboratory analysis shows serum lipase elevated to more than three times the upper limit of normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

opts.t: Acute pancreatitis related to ERCP procedure

expl: Epigastric pain to the back with lipase >3× normal hours after ERCP = post-ERCP pancreatitis, the commonest ERCP complication.

stem: A 55-year-old man presents with recurrent epigastric pain, steatorrhea, and new-onset diabetes. CT scan shows pancreatic calcifications. What is the most likely diagnosis?
srcNote: (Pancreas)
expl: Chronic epigastric pain + exocrine failure (steatorrhoea) + endocrine failure (diabetes) + pancreatic calcifications = chronic pancreatitis.

stem: A 35-year-old female presents with signs and symptoms of acute pancreatitis. Abdominal ultrasound reveals gallstones and a dilated common bile duct, consistent with biliary obstruction. There is no gallbladder wall thickening, no pericholecystic fluid, and no evidence of acute cholangitis. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
expl: Source key A. Gallstone pancreatitis with a dilated CBD on US suggests a retained/obstructing stone → ERCP to clear the duct. (Without cholangitis, many surgeons first confirm with MRCP/EUS; ERCP is clearly indicated with cholangitis or persistent obstruction.)

why.B: Diagnostic alternative when the stone is uncertain.

stem: A 50-year-old man with a history of chronic alcohol use presents with chronic epigastric pain and steatorrhea. Imaging shows dilated pancreatic ducts consistent with chronic pancreatitis. What is the most appropriate long-term management for symptom control?

opts.t: Alcohol cessation and pancreatic enzyme replacement
Long-term opioid therapy as primary treatment
Endoscopic ductal stenting as initial therapy

srcNote: (Pancreas)
expl: First-line in chronic alcoholic pancreatitis: stop alcohol (and smoking), pancreatic enzyme replacement for steatorrhoea, analgesia, diabetes control. Surgery/endoscopy for refractory pain.

why.C: Opioids are not the primary treatment (dependence).

stem: The patient came with epigastric pain and vomiting, he had acute pancreatitis 6 weeks ago which was treated conservatively. CT scan showed a 7cm lesion. His WBCs are normal, the patient is afebrile. Which of the following is the best treatment?
srcNote: (Confirmed by doctor) (Pancreas)
expl: A symptomatic 7-cm pseudocyst at 6 weeks (mature wall), afebrile → endoscopic transgastric drainage (current gold standard), confirmed by the doctor.

why.C: For failed endoscopic drainage or complications.

stem: A 50-year-old man with a history of acute pancreatitis two weeks ago presents with fever and abdominal pain. CT scan shows a peripancreatic solid collection with gas bubbles. What is the most appropriate management?

opts.t: IV Antibiotic Resuscitation and CT guided aspiration

srcNote: (Confirmed by doctor) (Pancreas)
expl: Doctor-confirmed key C. Early (2 weeks) infected necrosis (gas bubbles) → resuscitation, IV antibiotics (carbapenem) and CT-guided aspiration/drainage; necrosectomy is delayed (walled-off necrosis ~4+ weeks) because early surgery has high mortality.

stem: A 45-year-old man was admitted 10 days ago with acute pancreatitis. He is now afebrile and a follow-up CT shows a peripancreatic fluid collection without a well-formed capsule. What is the most appropriate management?
srcNote: (Pancreas)
expl: An acute peripancreatic fluid collection (<4 weeks, no wall) in an afebrile patient usually resolves → supportive care and observation.

why.B: Not indicated for sterile, early collections.

stem: A patient with chronic pancreatitis presents with steatorrhea. What is the most likely cause?
expl: Steatorrhoea in chronic pancreatitis = loss of exocrine (lipase) function (>90% of the gland destroyed).

why.D: Contributes, but the cause is exocrine insufficiency.

stem: What is the most common cause of acute pancreatitis?
expl: Gallstones are the commonest cause of acute pancreatitis worldwide (alcohol second).

stem: A patient diagnosed with pancreatitis a few weeks ago is now found to have a pseudocyst. Which condition indicates the need for surgical intervention?
expl: Source key A. A pseudocyst causing gastric/duodenal outlet obstruction is an indication for intervention (surgical/endoscopic drainage). Splenic artery pseudoaneurysm is treated by angio-embolisation; splenic vein thrombosis doesn't by itself need surgery.

why.D: Also an indication, but obstruction was keyed.

stem: A patient is diagnosed with mild acute pancreatitis. What is the most appropriate management?

opts.t: TPN, IV fluids, pain control, antibiotics
Enteral feeding, IV fluids, pain control

srcNote: Incomplete choice set: only two options are provided in the source.
expl: Mild AP → IV fluids (LR), analgesia and early enteral (oral) feeding. TPN and prophylactic antibiotics are not indicated.

why.A: TPN and antibiotics are not indicated.

stem: A patient presented with acute epigastric pain and high amylase level (case basically suggests acute pancreatitis) upon physical examination there was a dark discoloration on the patient's flanks. What's the name of this clinical sign?
srcNote: Source note (Midterm 431 A Q12): Grey Turner's sign is an uncommon subcutaneous manifestation of intra-abdominal pathology that manifests as ecchymosis or discoloration of the flanks Cullen’s appear around the umbilicus
expl: Flank ecchymosis = Grey Turner's sign (retroperitoneal haemorrhage tracking to the flanks) in haemorrhagic pancreatitis. Cullen's = periumbilical.

stem: A 38-year-old woman who was conservatively treated for acute pancreatitis 5 weeks ago. presented to the ER complaining of epigastric pain and postprandial vomiting. Physical examination revealed tenderness and fullness in the epigastric region. Blood pressure 115/65 mmHg Heart rate 82 /min Temperature 36.6 (afebrile) Respiratory rate 17/min Test Result (Normal value) WBC 8.9 (4-10.5 x 10 9 L) Serum amylase 4.9 (0.54-2.02 nkat/L) Abdominal US: Fluid collection surrounded by wall in the lesser sac 15 x 17 cm in size. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
srcNote: (Hepato-bilio-pancreatic neoplasms) (Acute and chronic pancreatitis)
expl: Weeks after AP, epigastric pain, post-prandial vomiting and an epigastric mass = pseudocyst compressing the stomach.

stem: 60 y o female with a history of multiple emergency visits, come to ER with epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. She had a history of cholecystectomy 30 years ago. She had a history of alcohol intake for a long time. High amylase and lipase with normal bilirubin.What is the diagnosis?
expl: Long-standing alcohol, previous cholecystectomy (gallstones unlikely) and normal bilirubin → alcoholic pancreatitis.

stem: Alcoholic patient was diagnosed with severe acute pancreatitis and was treated accordingly. 2 months later he presented with abdominal distension and positive shifting dullness and thrill test. Which of the following would confirm the etiology of the Ascites?
srcNote: ( necrotic pancreatitis ) Incomplete choice set: only two options are provided in the source.
expl: Source key B (CT). The classic test confirming pancreatic ascites is diagnostic paracentesis showing very high ascitic amylase (~3,000); CT shows the duct disruption/collections. Follow the key, but know the ascitic amylase.

stem: A 45-year-old male presents to your emergency department with acute episodic pain radiating to the back, the patient is febrile 38.8 and his serum amylase is 1854 U/L. Which one of the following is the most important initial imaging modality to confirm the cause?
srcNote: (Acute abdomen) Source note (Midterm 435 F Q9): This presentation is not necessarily pancreatitis because cholecystitis could also cause pain that radiates to the back and also serum amylase is not specific to pancreatitis unlike serum lipase
expl: Fever with back pain and high amylase → abdominal ultrasound is the key initial imaging to find the cause (gallstones/cholecystitis, CBD). The source notes that amylase isn't specific — cholecystitis also fits.

why.A: Excludes perforation, but doesn't find the cause.

stem: a 32-year-old woman admitted to the ICU with severe pancreatitis complicated by sepsis. On examination, she was having generalized edema with hypertension despite infusion of large amount of intravenous ringer lactate. Which of the following is the most likely body fluid abnormality the patient may have?
srcNote: (Principles of fluids and electrolytes balance in surgical patient)
expl: In severe pancreatitis/sepsis, capillary leak moves fluid into the interstitium (third space) → edema despite fluids. Same question as 48e7a343 with "hypertension" (likely a typo for hypotension).

why.A: The interstitium is overloaded, not depleted.

stem: A 35-year-old man came to the emergency department complaining of acute epigastric pain radiating to his back associated with vomiting six times. On abdominal examination he is tender in the epigastrium and right upper quadrant, his temperature is 39 C, Serum Amylase is 2500 U/L What is the most likely diagnosis?
srcNote: (acute abdomen)
expl: Acute epigastric pain radiating to the back with repeated vomiting and epigastric tenderness = acute pancreatitis (confirm with lipase/amylase).

stem: A 28-year-old woman who is known to have multiple small gallstones, presented to the ER complaining of severe epigastric pain associated with vomiting for 18 hours. Physical examination revealed upper abdominal tenderness. Blood pressure 120/65 mmHg Heart rate 86 /min Temperature 37.8 Respiratory rate 18/min Test Result: (Normal value) WBC 13.4 (4-10.5 x 10 9 L) Serum amylase 5.4 (0.54-2.02 nkat/L) Alkaline phosphatase 3.2 (0.7-1.9 ukat/L) Total bilirubin 34 (3.5-16.5 umol/L) Direct bilirubin 19 (1.5-6.5 umol/L) Which of the following is the appropriate initial management?
srcNote: ? (Gallstone related disorders, Acute and chronic pancreatitis) Uncertain source key: the original answer includes a question mark.
expl: Source key C (marked "?"). Gallstone pancreatitis without cholangitis (stable, no fever, mild cholestasis) → initial management is IV crystalloid resuscitation; ERCP only if cholangitis/persistent obstruction; US to confirm the cause.

stem: A 47-year-old man presented to the emergency department complaining of severe epigastric pain for 3 days associated win frequent retching and vomiting, on examination, he was dehydrated , heart rate: 105 beat/ minute, blood pressure 100/65 mmHg, marked tenderness in the epigastric region. Blood test revealed serum amylase 1433 (normal <117) normal liver function test. Ultrasound revealed multiple small gallstones. CT scan abdomen showed necrotizing acute pancreatitis with gas bubbles Which of the following is best indicated?
srcNote: (Gallstone related disorders) (Acute and chronic pancreatitis)
expl: Necrotising pancreatitis with gas bubbles = infected necrosis → IV antibiotics (carbapenem) first; necrosectomy is delayed (step-up approach). Emergency laparotomy has high mortality.

why.D: FNA is possible, but gas already confirms infection.

stem: A 38-year-old woman presented to emergency department complaining of severe epigastric pain associated with vomiting for 18 hours. Physical examination revealed upper abdominal tenderness. Laboratory values showed white blood cell count of 14 x910 and serum amylase of 1738 IU (normal value < 117 IU). Which of the following is an expected complication of this condition?
srcNote: (Acute and chronic pancreatitis)
expl: Acute pancreatitis → hypocalcaemia (fat saponification), a Ranson criterion.

stem: A 35 years old man came to ER with epigastric pain and vomiting for 5 days , HR=100 BP 100/65 elevated WBC and Amylase , what is the initial investigation of choice?
srcNote: The repeated source note is an abbreviated exam recall; no full question or options are supplied for that reference. Source note (Final 435 F Q50 (p. 152)): Any acute pancreatitis like scenario where no Erect x ray was mentioned to be done, it will be the right ans.
expl: In any pancreatitis-like scenario where perforation hasn't been excluded, the first investigation is an erect chest X-ray (air under the diaphragm). The source note: if no erect CXR was mentioned, it's the answer.

stem: A 44-year-old woman presented to the emergency department complaining of epigastric pain for 2 days associated with frequent episodes of retching and vomiting. On examination, she was dehydrated, heart rate: 93 beat/ minute, blood pressure: 105/62 mmHg, mild tenderness in the epigastric region. Blood test revealed serum amylase of 1254 (Normal value < 117 1U) Which of the following blood tests be used to assess the severity of the disease?
expl: CRP (>150 mg/L at 48 h) is a severity marker in AP. Lipase/amylase confirm the diagnosis but don't reflect severity.

stem: A 38-year-old man who had a history of recurrent acute pancreatitis over the last 10 years presented to the ER complaining of frequent episodes of vomiting fresh blood for 12 hours. Intravenous resuscitation was initiated. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy: isolated bleeding fundal varices which has been controlled by injection sclerotherapy. US: Splenomegaly, normal portal vein and thrombosed splenic vein. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
srcNote: d (Acute and chronic pancreatitis)
expl: Recurrent pancreatitis → splenic vein thrombosis → left-sided (sinistral) portal hypertension → isolated gastric (fundal) varices with a normal portal vein → splenectomy is curative. (Source key "d".)

stem: A 38 year old woman presented to the emergency department with a history of epigastric abdominal pain for 5 days radiating to the back, associated with frequent vomiting. She is known to have multiple gallstones. Physical examination revealed diffuse abdominal distension and tenderness with sluggish bowel sounds. Laboratory values including complete blood count, liver function tests were all normal. Erect chest X-ray showed left pleural effusion Which of the following is the most appropriate initial investigation?
srcNote: (Acute and chronic pancreatitis)
expl: After 5 days serum amylase may normalise but urinary amylase stays raised (~10 days) → urine amylase. CT is used when diagnosis is still uncertain.

stem: 34 year old man presented to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain for 12 hours Physical examination revealed upper abdominal tenderness serum amylase: 250 IU/dl. Chest X-ray was normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
srcNote: (Acute and chronic pancreatitis) Conflicting source keys in similar recalls: the retained question gives CT; the 435 F and undated versions give ultrasound. Their original keys are preserved below. Other source key (Final 435 F Q33 (p. 148)): Ans: A (US) Other source key (Final Year not stated Q64 (p. 272)): Answer: C (Abdominal us)
expl: Source key A (CT) for confirming the diagnosis when amylase is only mildly raised; other versions of this recall keyed ultrasound. CT confirms pancreatitis when biochemistry is equivocal.

why.D: The other versions' key (for the cause).

stem: A 38-year-old woman who was conservatively treated for acute pancreatitis 5 weeks ago, presented to emergency department complaining of epigastric pain and postprandial vomiting. On examination, she was febrile 38.4 with tenderness and fullness in the epigastric region. Laboratory values showed high white blood cell count and amylase was: 645 IU/L (normal value < 117 IU/L. Ultrasound showed fluid collection surrounded by thick wall in the lesser sac 15*17 cm. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
expl: Source key C (435). A symptomatic pseudocyst after 5 weeks → drainage. The doctor's notes now prefer endoscopic transgastric drainage (the 442 doctor-confirmed key).

stem: a 27-year-old man admitted 8 weeks ago with severely infected necrotizing pancreatitis. He underwent several interventions for sepsis control and he was on mechanical ventilator and inotropes. Which of the following physiological changes is expected?
srcNote: the Question is not clear but the normal physiological response to inflammation is insulin-resistance increase and Glucagon secretion increase Conflicting source keys: the retained source gives B (Glucagon); the repeated 433 A recall gives A (Insulin). The source also describes the question as unclear. Other source key (Midterm 433 A Q51): Answer: A ( Miscellaneous ) the Question is not clear but the normal physiological response to inflammation is insulin-resistance increase and Glucagon secretion increase
expl: The stress response to severe prolonged sepsis raises catabolic hormones — glucagon, cortisol, catecholamines — with insulin resistance. Source key (434): glucagon.

why.A: Insulin levels may rise but tissues are resistant.

stem: Patient with necrotizing pancreatitis. What is the physiological abnormalities?
expl: Severe systemic inflammation → catabolism: increased lipolysis, increased gluconeogenesis and insulin resistance → hyperglycaemia.

stem: Patients with epigastric pain that radiates to the back with high amylase and mild dehydrated ( acute pancreatitis )What is the abnormality that will appear in his blood ?
srcNote: Source key was B; corrected — see explanation. Source key reproduced as written: B (hypoglycemia).
expl: The source key was B (hypoglycaemia), but the doctor's notes state glucose RISES initially in acute pancreatitis (stress hormones, islet injury) → hyperglycaemia; hypocalcaemia is the other classic finding.

why.B: Source key, contradicted by the doctor's notes.
why.C: Possible with vomiting, but not the classic answer.

stem: A 38 year old man comes to ER with severe abdominal pain and vomiting. The pain is radiating to his back and is improved by bending forward. Physical exam reveals tenderness over the epigastrium. An abdominal CT shows diffuse pancreatic enlargement with areas of necrosis. Which of the following work up determines the prognosis?
expl: Source key A. WBC >16,000 is a Ranson criterion, so it contributes to prognosis; calcium (<8 mg/dL at 48 h) is also a Ranson criterion. Lipase only confirms diagnosis.
